## Definitions

- [statement] Protein redistribution means limiting protein at breakfast and lunch while shifting intake toward dinner. It may improve levodopa response in selected patients with motor fluctuations, but definitions, patient selection and treatment algorithms lack consensus and high-level evidence is limited. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-023-00541-w · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Diet and nutrition in PD: Mediterranean, MIND, protein redistribution, ketogenic
- [statement] Multidisciplinary PD care is a patient-centered, needs-based model involving different professionals; the Parkinson Foundation describes experts working as needed across symptoms, while one randomized specialist-team model combined a movement-disorders specialist, PD nurses, and a social worker. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/finding-care · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23165981/

## Structure and components

- [statement] Burden scales can structure assessment: the 2024 meta-analysis identified the ZBI as the most used measure, and the 2025 predictor review also found it used more often than the other listed scales. Scores should be interpreted alongside the caregiver’s own account because validated measures may miss aspects of lived experience. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38573387/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12069830/
- [statement] In the 2018 pilot, ketogenic diet produced a larger improvement in MDS-UPDRS Part 1 nonmotor experiences than low-fat diet; there were no significant between-group differences in Parts 2 to 4. Within-group motor improvements do not establish ketogenic superiority. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6175383/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Diet and nutrition in PD: Mediterranean, MIND, protein redistribution, ketogenic
- [statement] In an 8-week pilot randomized trial, 47 people were randomized to low-fat or ketogenic diets and 38 completed. Ketogenic participants improved more on MDS-UPDRS Part 1 nonmotor experiences, but there were no between-group differences in Parts 2–4; intermittent worsening of tremor or rigidity was the most common ketogenic adverse effect. These results do not establish motor superiority or long-term safety. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6175383/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Diet and nutrition in PD: Mediterranean, MIND, protein redistribution, ketogenic
- [statement] Advance care planning includes clarifying values, choosing a surrogate, discussing future medical care and documenting preferences; paperwork is one part of the process. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6556088/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Palliative and advance care planning in PD · also: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/recommendations

## How it works

- [statement] The 2026 alcohol review explicitly advises that neither alcohol consumption nor smoking can be recommended for PD prevention because of their overall health harms. Apparent inverse epidemiologic associations should not be translated into advice to start either exposure. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13067329/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] Observational associations require consideration of confounding and reverse causation, including changes in exposure during prodromal PD. Courage-PD used genetic instruments to address these biases and supported an inverse smoking association, while explicitly leaving coffee and alcohol conclusions uncertain because of limited power. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9211765/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5664303/
- [statement] PD falls have multiple contributors: postural instability and gait dysfunction, including freezing, matter, and orthostatic hypotension can cause dizziness, syncope or unexplained falls. A fall assessment should therefore consider blood-pressure-related causes as well as mobility. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7220277/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7592655/
- [statement] A small prospective observational study of 30 people with PD found fewer outdoor falls and fall injuries among rollator users. Participants used rollators only outdoors, and the study could not adjust for other factors because of its small sample; it does not establish causal protection, indoor benefit or superiority of a particular model. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9984883/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] Orthostatic-hypotension assessment includes blood-pressure measurements supine and after three minutes standing, plus assessment of possible causes such as hypovolemia or blood-pressure-lowering drugs. This is relevant when falls are unexplained or accompanied by standing-related symptoms. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7592655/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation advises avoiding driving when fatigued, when medication is wearing off, or when starting a new medicine. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/activities-daily-living/driving · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] The national virtual-visit trial used a motor assessment that excluded rigidity and balance; the authors also identified difficulties assessing gait because of technology, camera view, and the absence of trained clinicians. Remote follow-up therefore leaves examination gaps. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] Advance care planning is a continuing discussion of future care needs, wishes and preferences, including decisions for a time when a person may be unable to decide independently. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8355553/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Palliative and advance care planning in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13771020/
- [statement] Individual readiness and timing matter: interview findings support regularly revisiting information preferences, while the PD_Pal contextual analysis found both resistance when discussion felt premature and cognitive limitations that could obstruct later participation. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8355553/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Palliative and advance care planning in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13771020/
- [statement] PD_Pal’s authors identify fragmented electronic-record documentation and limited visibility as possible reasons recorded preferences may be missed; documentation alone may not capture the quality or process of ACP discussions. ## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] Courage-PD estimated OR 0.74 (95% CI 0.60–0.93) for PD per standard-deviation increase in genetically predicted smoking initiation. It found no significant coffee or alcohol association but cautioned that conclusions for those two exposures were limited by insufficient statistical power. MR interpretation depends on valid instrumental-variable assumptions. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9211765/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] In Café-PD, 121 people with established PD were randomized to caffeine 200 mg twice daily or placebo. Caffeine did not significantly improve the primary motor outcome at six months; early modest sleepiness improvement attenuated over time, and secondary outcomes included slightly worse cognitive scores and increased dyskinesia. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5664303/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] Protein redistribution requires nutritional and medication monitoring: the 2023 practical review advises avoiding low-protein diets below 0.8 g/kg/day to prevent lean-mass loss, monitoring weight and dyskinesias, and considering levodopa dose adjustment when bioavailability improves. Its minimum is not a universal optimal protein prescription. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-023-00541-w · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Diet and nutrition in PD: Mediterranean, MIND, protein redistribution, ketogenic
- [statement] The 2017 national trial randomized 195 people and added 4 virtual specialist visits over 1 year to usual care. It reported 98% completing at least one virtual visit, 91% of scheduled virtual visits completed, and median savings of 88 minutes and 38 miles per visit. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5595275/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] The 2020 caffeine meta-analysis reported a progression association from cohort endpoints such as dyskinesia, motor fluctuation and levodopa initiation, but explicitly noted that none of its included studies isolated pure caffeine tablets and that an optimal caffeine dose could not be defined. Its pooled progression association should not be treated as randomized evidence of disease modification. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7353179/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] In a one-year randomized trial in early PD, transdermal nicotine did not slow progression. Of 163 randomized participants, 101 contributed to the primary endpoint; discontinuation and adverse events were important causes of dropout, and application-site skin reactions were common. The result does not support prescribing nicotine to slow established PD. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38320207/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] A 2026 UK Biobank analysis reported no overall coffee–PD association, but associations differed by CYP1A2 genotype: below 5 cups/day was associated with lower risk in AA carriers, whereas at least 5 cups/day was associated with higher risk in AC and CC carriers. The authors explicitly describe these observational findings as hypothesis-generating and noncausal. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-026-01519-0 · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] Lower PD incidence associated with coffee consumption should be distinguished from treating established PD: EPIC4PD observed an inverse risk association, while Café-PD found no clinically important motor benefit from caffeine treatment. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11175631/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5664303/
- [statement] Alcohol findings in Mendelian randomization studies conflict: Dominguez-Baleon and colleagues reported lower PD risk with genetically predicted alcohol intake (OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65–0.96), whereas Courage-PD found no significant association (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.39–1.18) and emphasized insufficient statistical power. Neither result alone establishes a preventive drinking recommendation. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8263722/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9211765/
- [statement] A 2025 review of forty-one studies identified the impact of motor symptoms on daily activities and severity of neuropsychiatric symptoms as burden predictors, but found evidence inconclusive for disease stage, duration and motor symptom severity; stage or duration alone should therefore not be used as a universal burden rule. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12069830/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] A Parkinson’s News Today feature describes irritability, exhaustion and low patience as burnout warning signs and illustrates the value one care partner places on specific offers of practical help. This is a reported personal experience and support guidance, not a validated diagnostic rule or causal trial. (low confidence) — https://parkinsonsnewstoday.com/avoiding-parkinsons-care-partner-burnout/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Reviews differ on disease duration and severity: a 2024 review reported higher burden with longer duration and greater severity, whereas Lesley and colleagues’ 2025 predictor review judged disease duration, stage and motor severity inconclusive. These should not be presented as universal independent predictors. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38573387/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12069830/
- [statement] The evidence base underrepresents some care partners: the 2025 review calls for younger and non-spousal caregivers and more diverse samples, while its limitations describe predominantly older female spouses and recruitment biased toward outpatient settings. Generalization to all caregiver relationships and disease stages requires caution. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12069830/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] The telephone CBT trial excluded possible dementia or marked cognitive impairment (Montreal Cognitive Assessment score <21), active suicidal plans or intent, unstable serious illness, and primary psychotic, bipolar, or substance-use disorder; its results therefore do not establish efficacy for these excluded groups. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] The Fox study cannot establish causation or longitudinal slowing of PD: progression was estimated from current symptoms and diagnosis date, and the authors explicitly acknowledged the cross-sectional limitation. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9739738/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Diet and nutrition in PD: Mediterranean, MIND, protein redistribution, ketogenic
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation says targeted nutrition may slow PD advancement, whereas the randomized-trial review describes efficacy evidence as inconclusive. Attribute the optimistic guidance and the evidentiary limitation explicitly; neither establishes disease modification. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/diet-nutrition · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Diet and nutrition in PD: Mediterranean, MIND, protein redistribution, ketogenic · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40879243/
- [statement] Mediterranean and MIND patterns emphasize plant foods, olive oil, fish and nuts and discourage red meat and sweets. MIND scoring additionally emphasizes leafy greens, berries and whole grains and penalizes butter, cheese and fried foods; different scoring scales cannot be compared as equivalent dose units. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9739738/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Diet and nutrition in PD: Mediterranean, MIND, protein redistribution, ketogenic
- [statement] The MIND/Mediterranean symptom analysis cannot establish causality: its authors describe a cross-sectional method, lack of temporal analysis, a largely white and wealthy US sample, possible co-occurring protective behaviors and unvalidated brief questionnaire scales. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9739738/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Diet and nutrition in PD: Mediterranean, MIND, protein redistribution, ketogenic
- [statement] In the PDSAFE randomized trial, the programme did not reduce falling overall, despite improvements in balance, falls efficacy and chair-stand time and fewer near falls. Secondary subgroup findings suggested different responses by disease severity. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6585265/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] For stairs, the Parkinson’s Foundation recommends clear, non-skid, well-lit steps and handrails; it advises avoiding ladders, step stools and chairs for climbing because balance and protective reflex changes increase fall risk. - [statement] The 2026 Canoro narrative review identifies augmentation bias: telemedicine arms may receive more clinical attention than controls, so improvement cannot automatically be attributed to video delivery itself. The authors regard efficiency evidence and long-term economic sustainability as unresolved. - [statement] The 2020 integrated-care review found only a small quality-of-life benefit in its outpatient subgroup; substantial overall heterogeneity and risk of bias limit generalization to all multidisciplinary models. - [statement] The 2020 randomized trial enrolled 210 people with PD or related disorders with moderate-to-high palliative needs; at 6 months the palliative-care group had better quality of life (treatment effect 1.87; 95% CI 0.47–3.27). Its mixed diagnostic population and selected needs limit extrapolation to all PD patients. ## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Prospective observational evidence frequently associates habitual caffeine or coffee consumption with lower incident PD risk: the 2020 cohort meta-analysis reported HR 0.797 (95% CI 0.748–0.849), and EPIC4PD also reported an inverse association. These are risk associations rather than intervention effects. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7353179/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11175631/
- [statement] In the 2024 EPIC4PD analysis of 184,024 participants, the highest coffee-intake category versus nonconsumption had adjusted HR 0.63 (95% CI 0.46–0.88). Its nested study of 351 incident cases and 351 controls associated higher prediagnostic caffeine, paraxanthine and theophylline with lower subsequent PD risk; adjustment for smoking and alcohol did not substantially change results. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11175631/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] In Café-PD, caffeine 200 mg twice daily did not improve the six-month motor outcome versus placebo in established PD. Sixty participants received caffeine and 61 placebo; the between-group MDS-UPDRS-III difference was −0.48 points (95% CI −3.21 to 2.25). This treatment result does not test primary prevention. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5664303/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] The 2023 correction to Hong’s caffeine meta-analysis fixed citation numbers in tables and figures; the authors stated that the scientific conclusions were unaffected. It should be consulted alongside the original meta-analysis rather than described as a retraction. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9919867/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] Two Mendelian randomization studies reported inverse smoking-related associations with PD, but for different exposures: Courage-PD found an association for genetic liability to smoking initiation, whereas Dominguez-Baleon and colleagues found an association for smoking continuation (current versus former smokers). These estimates do not identify nicotine as the responsible component. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9211765/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8263722/
- [statement] Nicotine has not demonstrated clinical benefit as a PD treatment: a randomized early-PD trial found that one year of transdermal nicotine did not slow progression, and a 2025 meta-analysis found no significant pooled short- or long-term motor improvement. The meta-analysis includes the trial and is corroborating synthesis rather than an independent replication. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38320207/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12384040/
- [statement] A patient-education RCT involving 46 care partners found short-term improvements in psychosocial problems and need for help after eight weekly sessions. A separate formative evaluation found improvements in those domains but none on health-state, quality-of-life or depression measures; outcomes should be reported by domain rather than as a blanket improvement in well-being. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19674927/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2804793/
- [statement] Evidence on cognition requires qualification: the scoping review described cognitive impairment as a consistent burden predictor, while the 2025 review restricted to multivariable analyses found general cognitive function did not predict burden. These differently scoped findings should remain attributed rather than collapsed into a universal cognitive-score rule. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10802092/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12069830/
- [statement] Caregiver burden describes adverse effects on caregivers’ physical, emotional, social and financial well-being; it should be assessed as the care partner’s own experience rather than equated with the person with PD being a burden. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10802092/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12069830/
- [statement] Poorer caregiver mental health and greater patient neuropsychiatric symptom severity are associated with greater burden. The 2025 predictor review also identified the impact of motor symptoms on daily living, rather than motor symptoms alone, as a consistent predictor. These observational findings do not establish causality. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12069830/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38573387/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10802092/
- [statement] Practical support should address the care partner’s own unmet needs, including psychosocial help and opportunities for respite; these are support priorities described in the literature, rather than a guarantee that any particular service will reduce burden. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10802092/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] In a randomized trial of 72 people with PD and depression, a 10-session telephone CBT intervention added to usual care improved Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores by 6.53 points versus −0.27 with usual care; benefits persisted during six-month follow-up that included monthly CBT contacts. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] Mindfulness-based yoga and meditation trials in mild-to-moderate PD suggest benefits for depressive symptoms compared with stretching and resistance exercise, but these programs and selected trial populations differ, so a single effect size should not be generalized across them. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6583059/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9862216/
- [statement] The mindfulness-yoga trial reported greater anxiety, depression and health-related quality-of-life improvement than stretching/resistance exercise, with similar physical benefits. Yoga classes lasted 90 minutes versus 60 minutes for controls. Unblinded participants, convenience sampling and exclusion of severe motor limitations restrict attribution and generalization. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6583059/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] In a 136-person trial, eight weeks of computerized cognitive training did not improve the primary planning-accuracy outcome or subjective cognitive complaints compared with an active control. A secondary processing-speed improvement had limited clinical impact, and no group differences remained at six months. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35248830/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] At one- and two-year COGTIPS follow-up, cognitive training showed no advantage on neuropsychological outcomes or conversion of cognitive status compared with an active control. Missing assessments, particularly during COVID-19 restrictions, limit interpretation. The result concerns the studied eight-week program. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10724826/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] PD-adapted CBT can improve depressive and anxiety symptoms compared with usual care or other control conditions; trial effects should not be interpreted as proof that every patient benefits. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12447579/
- [statement] The Cochrane review summary reported seven studies and 225 participants with PD-related mild cognitive impairment or dementia: it found no evidence of global-cognition improvement, and apparent attention/verbal-memory benefits did not survive sensitivity analysis. Evidence certainty was low, so this is uncertainty about efficacy rather than proof of ineffectiveness. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33780379/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] In an observational analysis of 1205 participants, higher MIND and Mediterranean scores were associated with fewer patient-reported PD symptoms after adjustment for age, gender, income and years since diagnosis. This was an association with symptom scores, rather than a randomized demonstration of slowed progression. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9739738/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Diet and nutrition in PD: Mediterranean, MIND, protein redistribution, ketogenic
- [statement] The MED-PARK publication is a randomized trial protocol specifying 44 participants and six months of modified Mediterranean diet versus usual diet. Its planned outcomes and enrollment timeline must not be presented as efficacy results. (low confidence) — https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/15/10/e101946 · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Diet and nutrition in PD: Mediterranean, MIND, protein redistribution, ketogenic
- [statement] The 2018 low-fat versus ketogenic pilot randomized 47 people with PD; 44 started and 38 completed the study. The intervention lasted eight weeks. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6175383/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Diet and nutrition in PD: Mediterranean, MIND, protein redistribution, ketogenic
- [statement] A 2026 critical review concluded that no nutritional intervention had independently replicated, durable cognitive efficacy in established PD. It treats a Mediterranean-style pattern as a reasonable nutritional default rather than an established cognitive treatment. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13708064/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Diet and nutrition in PD: Mediterranean, MIND, protein redistribution, ketogenic
- [statement] The 2022 Cochrane review found that exercise probably reduces fall rate in mild to moderate PD by 26% (rate ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.63–0.87; 1456 participants, 12 studies; moderate-certainty evidence). This describes falls per unit time, rather than a 26% reduction in the number of people who fall. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9169540/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] Home exercise benefits cannot be assumed to extend unchanged to severe PD. PDSAFE and a separate minimally supervised exercise trial found severity-dependent responses; in the latter, the higher-severity subgroup had a nonsignificant trend toward more falls. Subgroup findings warrant caution rather than a claim that exercise invariably harms advanced PD. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6585265/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4335992/
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation recommends removing clutter and trip hazards, maintaining stable non-skid floors, improving lighting, creating wide walking paths, and keeping electrical cords out of walking routes. These are practical recommendations, rather than a quantified PD-specific intervention effect. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/activities-daily-living/home-safety · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] In the PDSAFE randomized trial, repeat falling at six months did not significantly improve: 61.5% in the intervention group versus 55% in controls (controlled OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.74–1.98). Balance, falls efficacy and chair stand time improved despite the negative primary fall outcome. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6585265/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD
- [statement] Exercise benefits should not be assumed to apply uniformly across PD severity: the Cochrane exercise evidence predominantly concerned mild to moderate disease, and PDSAFE subgroup analyses associated the intervention with an increased fall rate in the most severe group. The subgroup finding is a caution rather than proof that all exercise harms advanced PD. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9169540/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Fall prevention, home safety and mobility aids in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6585265/
- [statement] Travel guidance recommends carrying extra medication and keeping medication in carry-on luggage rather than depending on checked bags. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/management/traveling · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living · also: https://davisphinneyfoundation.org/blog/travel-with-greater-ease-parkinsons/
- [statement] In a 2014 randomized trial of 191 people with PD and daily-activity difficulties, a 10-week home occupational-therapy intervention improved self-perceived daily activity performance at 3 months compared with usual care without occupational therapy; the endpoint does not establish disease modification. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24726066/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] In a Parkinson’s UK forum discussion, one traveler with PD reported that advance wheelchair assistance helped with airport queues and walking; this is an individual experience rather than evidence that one itinerary is best for everyone. (low confidence) — https://forum.parkinsons.org.uk/t/long-distance-air-travel-uk-to-australia-advice-please/43760 · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Living well with PD: driving, work, travel and daily living
- [statement] A 2022 review of multidisciplinary rehabilitation versus conventional physiotherapy included 6 studies and 1260 participants and found no statistically significant difference in functionality, disability, or quality of life. This rehabilitation comparison should not be treated as testing every integrated specialist-care model. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8901313/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] In a 2025 case-control study of 490 people with PD and 140 healthy controls, digital exclusion was greater in PD, especially because of poorer digital skills; PD severity independently predicted exclusion. These observational associations identify an implementation barrier rather than proving that PD causes digital exclusion. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12625107/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] A 2024 randomized study of fifty participants evaluated additional nurse, neurologist, and occupational-therapist telemedicine alongside office visits, reporting less frailty and improved quality of life. This is evidence for that small hybrid program, rather than proof that any video visit improves outcomes. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39586130/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] A nurse-managed PD clinic demonstrated a hybrid service design combining an onsite team with remote movement-disorder expertise and multidisciplinary referral. Its implementation report establishes feasibility and access experience, rather than a controlled estimate of clinical effectiveness. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26055776/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Multidisciplinary care models and telemedicine in PD
- [statement] Lum and colleagues recommend starting ACP discussions early because later communication and cognitive difficulties can reduce participation; they also recommend checking readiness, knowledge and information needs rather than assuming everyone wants the same discussion. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6556088/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] In that 2020 trial, among participants without an advance directive at baseline, six-month completion was 53% with palliative care versus 26% with standard care; the health-care-proxy completion comparison was not significant. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7042842/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Palliative and advance care planning in PD
- [statement] In the 2021 qualitative interview study of 20 patients, most wanted ACP discussion with a clinician and the majority preferred clinician initiation early in the disease; preferred information timing varied. These are participant perspectives rather than evidence that everyone wants immediate detailed end-of-life planning. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8355553/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Palliative and advance care planning in PD

## Facts and statements

- [statement] The 2026 UK Biobank analysis reported no overall coffee–PD association in 435,551 participants with 3319 incident cases, whereas EPIC4PD reported an inverse association. The UK analysis reported differing associations by CYP1A2 genotype; these study-specific results should not be collapsed into a universal protective coffee effect. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-026-01519-0 · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11175631/
- [statement] In the UK Biobank study, coffee-by-CYP1A2 interaction was significant, but coffee-by-sex and the three-way coffee-by-genotype-by-sex interactions were not statistically significant. Sex-stratified differences therefore require caution. The authors also state that their coffee measure included decaffeinated coffee, preventing isolation of caffeine-specific exposure, and that this observational study does not establish causality. (low confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-026-01519-0 · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] Smoking is associated with lower PD incidence in epidemiologic research, and the Courage-PD Mendelian-randomisation analysis also supported an inverse association for genetic liability to smoking initiation. This exposure association does not establish nicotine treatment efficacy. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38320207/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9211765/
- [statement] The 2025 nicotine meta-analysis of five randomized trials and 346 participants found no significant short- or long-term motor benefit and no significant short-term improvement in daily functioning, cognition or quality of life, with considerable between-study heterogeneity. It does not establish preventive effects before diagnosis. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12384040/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] Alcohol–PD findings disagree across study designs and reference groups: NeuroEPIC4PD reported no overall baseline or lifetime alcohol association, whereas the 2026 systematic review reported inverse associations in several pooled observational comparisons and inconsistent MR evidence. Neither result establishes that starting alcohol prevents PD. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7496254/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13067329/
- [statement] The early-PD nicotine trial randomized 163 participants, but only 101 were assessed for the primary endpoint; discontinuation and adverse events contributed to dropout, and patch-site skin adverse effects were common. Attrition limits interpretation of the efficacy estimate. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38320207/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Caffeine, smoking, nicotine and alcohol associations with PD
- [statement] Care partner burden in PD encompasses effects on emotional and physical health, social participation and finances; caregiving can also be rewarding, so burden should not be assumed to define every relationship. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10802092/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12069830/
- [statement] Caregiver mental health warrants assessment in its own right: a cross-sectional baseline analysis of 175 patient-caregiver pairs associated caregiver depression and anxiety with burden, and a 2025 systematic review identified poorer caregiver mental health among predictors. These are associations, not proof that treating anxiety alone reduces burden. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31735048/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12069830/
- [statement] In interviews with 36 care partners across 11 European countries, participants described information needs distinct from those of the person with PD, especially medication management, side effects, contacts for problems and responses to behavioural or mental health symptoms. These qualitative findings describe needs, not intervention effectiveness. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10578036/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Practical support options include planned time away from caregiving, help from relatives or friends, social-work resource navigation and respite or in-home assistance; the Foundation recommends these options, and qualitative research documents care partners’ unmet need for time to themselves. This supports a needs-based support plan, without establishing a quantified treatment effect. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/blog/care/address-prevent-burnout · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10578036/
- [statement] Peer groups need a suitable format: the European interview study found mixed experiences, including reluctance to voice concerns in front of the person with PD; participants appreciated care-partner-specific groups. Generic support groups should not be assumed to meet everyone’s needs. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10578036/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] A small preliminary randomised trial enrolled 30 distressed care partners and compared 12–14 CBT sessions with no treatment; it reported greater improvement in psychological distress, strain and subjective burden, maintained over a further three-month follow-up. The authors called for larger studies and longer-term assessment. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1739584/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] CBT evidence for care-partner burden is mixed: the preliminary Secker–Brown trial reported improvement, whereas a 2024 meta-analysis reported no significant pooled burden reduction. The positive small trial does not establish a reliable general effect, and the pooled null result does not prove that no individual can benefit. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1739584/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38573387/
- [statement] The Parkinson’s Foundation care-partner page directs readers to its Helpline, local chapters, support groups and free self-paced care-partner courses. These are resource-navigation options; the page is not trial evidence for reducing burden. (low confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/resources-support/carepartners · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Care partnering includes emotional support as well as physical tasks, and the role changes as PD progresses; support planning should recognize this evolving involvement. (medium confidence) — https://www.parkinson.org/resources-support/carepartners · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12069830/
- [statement] In the PEPP randomized trial, sixty-four people with PD and 46 caregivers were allocated to education or usual care. Eight weekly 90-minute sessions improved caregivers’ psychosocial problems and need for help at assessment one week after completion; this short follow-up does not establish durable benefit. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19674927/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] A survey of 141 current and 15 former PD carers identified unmet needs around finding balance, relationship changes, and coping with reduced emotions and motivation. About half of current carers were interested in exchanging experience with former carers, and commonality with peers mattered. This was a needs-and-preferences study, not a trial proving burden reduction. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9569356/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD
- [statement] Psychoeducation and other caregiver support interventions are promising, but reliable long-term burden reduction is not established across programs. The scoping review identified small samples, inconsistent outcomes and limited longitudinal data; the 2024 meta-analysis found no significant pooled caregiver-burden effect for cognitive behavior therapy. Improvement in mood or coping should not be described automatically as improvement in burden. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10802092/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, Care partner support and caregiver burden in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38573387/
- [statement] PD-adapted CBT uses cognitive and behavioral coping skills. Depression protocols include behavioral activation, cognitive restructuring and anxiety management; anxiety protocols include psychoeducation, exposure, thought restructuring and home practice. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9290129/
- [statement] In Moonen and colleagues’ 48-person anxiety trial, ten weekly CBT sessions did not significantly outperform clinical monitoring on the primary Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale. The secondary Parkinson Anxiety Scale favored CBT, so outcome choice materially affects interpretation. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9290129/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] Gwak and Park’s 2026 anxiety meta-analysis reported a pooled benefit for psychological and mind–body interventions but rated overall evidence certainty very low. The prediction interval included no effect, and most comparisons used inactive controls. The mindfulness/mind–body subgroup interval included no effect; subgroup differences were not statistically established. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13685121/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] The PD-MCI group-training trial randomized 64 participants to six weeks of multidomain training or low-intensity physical activity; phonemic fluency improved significantly, but the overall executive-function interaction was only a statistical trend. The authors called for longitudinal studies before inferring slower cognitive decline. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7721510/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] Selected short-term cognitive-test gains should not be presented as proof of dementia prevention: the PD-MCI group-training study called for longitudinal testing, whereas COGTIPS found no long-term cognitive or cognitive-status conversion advantage. The studies used different populations and training protocols. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7721510/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10724826/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35248830/
- [statement] The 2025 CBT meta-analysis included 16 RCTs and 682 participants, with searches updated through February 29, 2024; it found pooled improvements in depression and anxiety but no statistically significant pooled quality-of-life improvement. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12447579/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] In the mindfulness-yoga trial, 138 participants received eight weeks of yoga or stretching/resistance exercise; the yoga program reduced anxiety and depressive symptoms and improved health-related quality of life, while motor dysfunction and mobility benefits were described as comparable to exercise. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6583059/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] In the 68-participant mindfulness-meditation trial, both meditation and exercise groups improved on cognitive performance immediately after treatment; meditation was not shown to provide a superior cognitive benefit. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9862216/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] Cognitive-training findings in PD are task-specific and inconsistent: one PD-MCI trial favored training on phonemic fluency, whereas a larger computerized-training trial found no benefit on its primary planning-accuracy outcome and no group differences at follow-up. These results do not establish broad or durable cognitive improvement. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7721510/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35248830/
- [statement] A stress-and-mindfulness viewpoint presented potential effects on PD progression as a hypothetical mechanistic framework informed partly by animal studies; this source does not demonstrate that mindfulness slows human PD progression. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7894549/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD
- [statement] Apparent treatment benefits need interpretation against control design and outcome choice: the telephone CBT investigators could not fully separate psychotherapy-specific effects from contact and attention, and the computerized cognitive-training investigators found only minor secondary gains with limited clinical impact despite a null primary outcome. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7282876/ · keywords: Parkinson's disease lifestyle and supportive care: diet and nutrition, caffeine, falls and home safety, daily living, CBT and cognitive training, palliative care, care partners and care models, CBT, mindfulness and cognitive training in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35248830/
- [statement] A varied whole-food diet that supplies adequate energy and protein is practical supportive care in PD; a Mediterranean-style pattern is a reasonable default, while meals should be individualized with a dietitian to nutritional needs and medication timing. - [statement] Dietary protein can reduce or delay levodopa effectiveness in some people with PD. - [statement] A single-center Mediterranean-diet trial randomized eighty people with idiopathic PD to diet or control for 10 weeks; 35 per group completed it.
